hints: Focus on what actually changes the value of Kp, not just the position of equilibrium.
Notice that the temperature is 700 K in both experiments, only the total pressure changes from 200 kPa to 1000 kPa.
Recall that for a given reaction, Kp stays constant if temperature is unchanged, even though higher pressure shifts this equilibrium to the right.
walkthrough:
**Recall what Kp depends on**

Think of Kp as a fingerprint for a reaction at a given temperature. It is only changed by a change in temperature, not by pressure, concentration or catalyst.

$$K_p \text{ depends only on } T \text{ (for a given reaction)}$$

**Compare the two conditions**

Both experiments are at the same temperature, 700 K. The only difference is total pressure, 200 kPa for Y and 1000 kPa for Z.

$$T_Y = T_Z = 700 \text{ K, so } K_{p,Y} \text{ must equal } K_{p,Z}$$

**Separate Kp from position of equilibrium**

Increasing pressure will shift the equilibrium to the right because there are 3 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles on the right.

$$2\text{SO}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3(g)$$

That gives more $\text{SO}_3$ at equilibrium, but the ratio defined by Kp stays exactly the same. So Y and Z are identical.

options.A: Correct. Kp changes only with temperature. Since temperature is 700 K in both cases, Y equals Z despite the pressure increase.
options.B: Incorrect. You may be thinking that higher pressure favours the reverse reaction or lowers Kp. In fact higher pressure shifts position to the right but does not change the value of Kp at constant T.
options.C: Incorrect. This trap confuses the equilibrium yield with the equilibrium constant. The value 2.2 has no meaning here, Kp does not scale with pressure in this way.
options.D: Incorrect. This is the common trap of scaling Kp with pressure (1000 / 200 = 5.0). Pressure changes the partial pressures at equilibrium, but their ratio in the Kp expression stays constant at the same temperature.
